statement: Session prescription (volume, intensity, paces) must come from deterministic engine code; an LLM may only produce explanatory text behind schema and rule validation.
Run an automated expert-style quality checklist on every generated plan (progression, recovery weeks, intensity distribution, taper, level differentiation); a failing plan is not published.

Require structured inputs before generation (recent training history, availability, goal and race date, recent race or hard-effort results); plan quality rose with input detail, so ask for more rather than guess.
Derive paces and thresholds from the athlete's own recent hard efforts and race results, not population percentages or device VO2max; refit as new data arrive.
appliesTo: Athletes with at least one recent hard effort or race

statement: Never set paces directly from a watch-reported VO2max; treat it as a smoothed trend with about plus or minus 10 ml/kg/min individual error and ignore resting-based estimates.

Project race times between distances with a runner-specific exponent or a two-parameter capacity/endurance model; fall back to a fixed power-law default (Riegel 1.06 is convention, not from these abstracts) only with results at one distance; present a range that widens for distances far from recent races (ultras).
appliesTo: Goal-time setting and race prediction, including ultra distances

statement: Re-predict the goal time and re-derive pacing guidance as new training or race data arrive, showing the change and uncertainty; pacing numbers are not justified by the cited papers and must come from other topic rules.
value: on each new qualifying hard effort or race

statement: Update individual parameters (fitness, load tolerance) by shrinking toward population priors and require repeated comparable observations before changing them; no single test or block changes the model on its own. The minimum count is a conservative default, not evidence-derived.
appliesTo: Individual adaptation of any model parameter

statement: Do not store a high/low/non-responder classification; if a block shows no measurable improvement beyond measurement noise, vary the training stimulus before drawing a conclusion.

If a CTL/ATL/TSB-style view is shown, use fixed population time constants (conventional 42 and 7 days, a convention not derived from these papers) and label it a descriptive trend; never fit per-athlete constants, and never present TSB as a precise readiness or taper-timing prediction.

No ACWR or other load-ratio band may gate, block or justify a progression decision or be marketed as injury prediction; if displayed, use an EWMA form, mark it low-confidence and descriptive. Progression is limited by explicit caps declared as expert rules with a conservative default (grade D, no numeric value justified here).

HRV readiness may only downgrade a planned hard session to easy after a sustained drop versus a rolling personal baseline; it never adds load and never drives plan structure. Window length is a default, as the best method is unestablished.
appliesTo: Athletes who opt in and have regular HRV recordings

statement: Any ML injury-risk indicator must be advisory (non-alarming heads-up) and must not alter the plan automatically; reported AUCs of 0.68 to 0.72 are insufficient for decisions.
Cohort or similar-runner data may seed typical weekly volume and long-run shape for a goal time as priors; results are clamped by explicit safety caps and never used as targets to exceed.
appliesTo: Initial plan seeding for athletes with limited history
